body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students connect the spread of Islam and the Arabic language to broader patterns of trade and empire (D2.His.1.6-8).
- Students classify the work of Baghdad's scholars as examples of continuity (preserving older knowledge) and change (new discoveries) (D2.His.2.6-8).
- Students explain how trade routes connected Baghdad to distant places and carried knowledge (D2.Geo.7.6-8).
- Students cite evidence from a primary source and determine the central ideas of secondary readings (RH.6-8.1, RH.6-8.2), and develop an explanation with well-chosen facts (WHST.6-8.2.B).
- Students evaluate the relative influence of trade and scholarship and organize evidence into an argument (D2.His.15.6-8, D2.His.16.6-8).

MATERIALS
- A Faith and an Empire Spread (lesson reading)
- Baghdad and the House of Wisdom (secondary reading)
- Al-Khwarizmi Explains Why He Wrote His Book (primary source)
- A map of the Abbasid Caliphate around 800 CE with major trade routes
- A continuity-and-change T-chart

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Map: locate Mecca, Medina, Damascus, Baghdad and Cordoba. Begin the lesson, A Faith and an Empire Spread. Set norms for studying religions respectfully: we describe what believers believe and what historians know.
Day 2: Finish the lesson. Read Baghdad and the House of Wisdom together; students sort its details on the continuity-and-change T-chart.
Day 3: Students complete The House of Wisdom source analysis in pairs, then write their claims individually.
Day 4: Students choose one idea and complete Ideas That Traveled On; quick gallery walk of the ideas chosen.
Day 5: Assessment: Baghdad's Golden Age.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a timeline strip (610, 622, 632, 661, 750, 762, 813-833, 1258) for students to keep beside the readings. Offer a claim frame: "Al-Ma'mun supported scholars because ___. Al-Khwarizmi shows this when he writes ___."
- Support: shorten Ideas That Traveled On to one idea with three linked steps (where it began, how it traveled, what changed).
- Stretch: compare the House of Wisdom with a later center of learning, such as Timbuktu (which students meet in Unit 4) or a medieval European university.
- Multilingual learners: point out English words borrowed from Arabic (algebra, algorithm, zero, coffee, sugar) and invite students to share related words from their own languages; provide a glossary of caliph, caliphate and hajj with images.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are studying the Islamic world from the 600s to the 1200s, when Baghdad was one of the great cities of the world and a center of science, mathematics and medicine. We study religions in history class by learning what believers believe and what historians know, always respectfully. Ask your child to tell you where the words algebra and algorithm come from, and why a ruler might pay scholars to translate books.
title: Teacher guide: The Islamic World
